Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.

- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
If you give me a thousand words, I don't want to spend them all at once. I want to lay them out like coins on a kitchen table in late afternoon light, and decide, slowly, what is worth buying. Not much, perhaps. A memory. A smell. A door left open.

The first thing that comes to me is a kitchen that probably never existed exactly as I remember it. Winter outside, condensation on the windows, and someone — a grandmother, maybe yours, maybe mine in the way stories lend us grandmothers — making soup from whatever was left. Carrots gone sweet from cooking too long. Bread warming. A radio playing low enough that you have to lean in to hear the weather. She tastes the broth and says, without looking up, that it needs patience more than salt. I have thought about that sentence for years, in kitchens and in traffic and in arguments I wanted to win too quickly. Most things do.

Then a train. Not a sleek one, but the kind that sighs at every station and lets the cold in each time the doors open. A man across from me holding a paper bag of oranges like they are fragile and important, which they are. A child pressing her forehead to the glass, making a small, foggy continent with her breath and then wiping it away with her sleeve. Nobody is going anywhere extraordinary. Work, home, a hospital visit, a birthday. And yet, for twenty minutes, we are all traveling in the same direction, agreeing silently not to make it harder for each other. That feels like a kind of civilization.

Then the sea, because it always arrives uninvited. Not postcard sea, but early morning sea before anyone has claimed it. Grey and silver, the beach combed by wind, a dog inventing urgent reasons to run. I think everyone should, once in a while, stand somewhere bigger than their worries and let it rearrange them. The ocean doesn't solve anything. It just reminds you that most things rise and fall and rise again without needing your permission.

I think of learning to ride a bicycle, and learning most other things after that. The wobble is the lesson. Someone running alongside, hand hovering at the back of the seat, promising not to let go and then, mercifully, lying. Because the moment you realize you have been balancing on your own, something in you quietly rearranges from "I can't" to "Oh. I can, badly, and then better." We spend the rest of our lives looking for that feeling disguised as other things: a first apartment, a difficult conversation handled gently, a piece of work finally finished.

If I could build a place out of these words, it would be a small city of second chances. There would be a shop for lost things, not just umbrellas and gloves and single earrings, but lost tempers, lost years, sentences we wish we could take back and sentences we wish we had said. You could walk in and ask, politely, if anyone had handed in your courage, circa last spring. The person behind the counter would check a drawer and say, "We have something very similar. Would you like to try it?" And it would fit, not perfectly, but enough to leave wearing it.

There would be benches built for lingering and libraries that stay open late for people who are not ready to go home to their own thoughts. There would be public apologies and private forgivenesses, both tax-free. Neighbors would trade excess: tomatoes for lemons, ladders for company, stories for silence.

I don't know why these are the things that come. No dragons, no grand revelations. Just soup and trains and the sea doing its old work. Maybe because a life is not mostly made of turning points. It is made of Tuesdays. It is made of remembering to buy milk, of texting "got home safe," of holding the elevator for someone carrying too much. The small acts are not decorations on a life. They are the life.

So if I have a thousand words, I will spend the last of them like this: thank you for the ordinary miracle of paying attention. Look up once today. Notice who is being kind without being asked. Be that person if you can, and if you can't today, let someone else be that person for you without apologizing for needing it. Add patience more than salt. Travel in the same direction for a while. Let go of the seat when it's time.

The rest, I think, will balance itself.
---
